specStatements.text: Energy is conserved in chemical reactions. The amount of energy in the universe at the end of a chemical reaction is the same as before the reaction takes place. If a reaction transfers energy to the surroundings the product molecules must have less energy than the reactants, by the amount transferred.
An exothermic reaction is one that transfers energy to the surroundings so the temperature of the surroundings increases.
Exothermic reactions include combustion, many oxidation reactions and neutralisation.
Everyday uses of exothermic reactions include self-heating cans and hand warmers.
An endothermic reaction is one that takes in energy from the surroundings so the temperature of the surroundings decreases.
Endothermic reactions include thermal decompositions and the reaction of citric acid and sodium hydrogencarbonate. Some sports injury packs are based on endothermic reactions.
Students should be able to:
distinguish between exothermic and endothermic reactions on the basis of the temperature change of the surroundings
evaluate uses and applications of exothermic and endothermic reactions given appropriate information.
Limited to measurement of temperature change. Calculation of energy changes or ΔH is not required.
Required practical 4: investigate the variables that affect temperature changes in reacting solutions such as, eg acid plus metals, acid plus carbonates, neutralisations, displacement of metals.

Chemical reactions can occur only when reacting particles collide with each other and with sufficient energy. The minimum amount of energy that particles must have to react is called the activation energy.
Reaction profiles can be used to show the relative energies of reactants and products, the activation energy and the overall energy change of a reaction.
Students should be able to:

draw simple reaction profiles (energy level diagrams) for exothermic and endothermic reactions showing the relative energies of reactants and products, the activation energy and the overall energy change, with a curved line to show the energy as the reaction proceeds
use reaction profiles to identify reactions as exothermic or endothermic
explain that the activation energy is the energy needed for a reaction to occur.
During a chemical reaction:
energy must be supplied to break bonds in the reactants
energy is released when bonds in the products are formed.
The energy needed to break bonds and the energy released when bonds are formed can be calculated from bond energies.

The difference between the sum of the energy needed to break bonds in the reactants and the sum of the energy released when bonds in the products are formed is the overall energy change of the reaction.
In an exothermic reaction, the energy released from forming new bonds is greater than the energy needed to break existing bonds.
In an endothermic reaction, the energy needed to break existing bonds is greater than the energy released from forming new bonds.

scopeNotes.statement: Limited to measurement of temperature change.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Every item drawn from 4.5.1.1, including Required practical 4, judges the direction of energy transfer from a temperature reading taken before and after the reaction. Students are asked to read or compare thermometer values and to say whether the surroundings warmed or cooled; no item asks for a quantity of energy to be worked out from that reading, and none uses mass, specific heat capacity or any energy expression.

scopeNotes.statement: Calculation of energy changes or ΔH is not required.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: No item uses the symbol ΔH or asks for an energy change to be calculated from experimental data. The one calculation in this topic, in item q26, is the higher-tier bond-energy sum that statements S21 and S22 require in 4.5.1.3; it is worked from a table of bond energies, not from a temperature change, and its answer is reported as an overall energy change in kJ/mol rather than as ΔH.

concepts.definition: Energy is conserved in chemical reactions: the amount of energy in the universe at the end of a chemical reaction is the same as before the reaction takes place. Energy is only moved between the reacting chemicals and their surroundings.

Everything outside the reacting chemicals themselves, including the solvent, the container and the air. It is the temperature of the surroundings that a thermometer in the reaction mixture actually measures.
A reaction that transfers energy to the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings increases. The product molecules end up with less energy than the reactants, by the amount transferred.
A reaction that takes in energy from the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings decreases.
The reaction of a substance with oxygen, releasing energy. Combustion is exothermic.
A reaction in which a substance gains oxygen. Many oxidation reactions, such as the slow oxidation of iron in a hand warmer, are exothermic.
The reaction of an acid with a base or alkali to form a salt and water. Neutralisation is exothermic.
The breaking down of a compound into simpler substances on heating, for example calcium carbonate into calcium oxide and carbon dioxide. Thermal decompositions are endothermic.
An everyday use of an exothermic reaction: a reaction in a separate compartment of the can transfers energy to the drink and warms it.
An everyday use of an exothermic reaction: iron powder oxidises slowly inside the pack and transfers energy to the surroundings.
A use of an endothermic reaction: the reaction inside the pack takes in energy from the surroundings, so the pack and the injury are cooled.
The rise or fall in temperature measured before and after a reaction. A rise shows an exothermic reaction; a fall shows an endothermic one.
An investigation of the variables that affect temperature changes in reacting solutions, such as acid plus metals, acid plus carbonates, neutralisations and displacement of metals.
Chemical reactions can occur only when reacting particles collide with each other and with sufficient energy; a collision with too little energy does not lead to a reaction.
The minimum amount of energy that particles must have to react. It is the energy needed for a reaction to occur.
An energy level diagram showing the relative energies of reactants and products, the activation energy and the overall energy change, with a curved line showing the energy as the reaction proceeds.
The difference in energy between the reactants and the products, shown on a reaction profile and, at higher tier, calculated from bond energies.
Energy must be supplied to break bonds in the reactants, so bond breaking takes energy in.
Energy is released when bonds in the products are formed.
The energy associated with a particular bond, used to calculate the energy needed to break bonds and the energy released when bonds are formed.

misconceptions.question: A beaker of reacting solution becomes hot. Is energy going into the chemicals or out of them?
misconceptions.correct: Out of them. The reaction is exothermic: energy is transferred from the chemicals to the surroundings, which is why the surroundings become hotter.
misconceptions.misconception: If something gets hot it must be taking energy in, so a reaction that heats a beaker is endothermic.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In everyday life things get hot because you heat them: a kettle, an oven, a radiator. Students carry that pattern across and assume the hot object is the one receiving energy, which reverses the two words.
misconceptions.correction: Ask which way energy moves relative to the surroundings. Exothermic sends energy out to the surroundings, and the thermometer is measuring the surroundings, so a rise means energy came out.

misconceptions.question: A neutralisation warms the solution in the beaker. Have the surroundings warmed up?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. The solvent, the beaker and the air around the reacting chemicals are all the surroundings, so the solution warming up is the surroundings warming up.
misconceptions.misconception: The surroundings means the room, so warming of the solution itself does not count as energy transferred to the surroundings.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word surroundings sounds like the space around the apparatus, so students exclude the water the chemicals are dissolved in, even though that is what the thermometer sits in.
misconceptions.correction: Define the system as the reacting chemicals only. Everything else, starting with the solvent, is the surroundings, which is why a thermometer in the mixture measures the surroundings.

misconceptions.question: In an exothermic reaction, what has happened to the energy that was released?
misconceptions.correct: It has been transferred to the surroundings, warming them. The total energy in the universe is unchanged.
misconceptions.misconception: The energy is used up or destroyed by the reaction.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students hear energy is lost as heat and take lost literally, so the energy leaves the accounts altogether instead of appearing in the surroundings.
misconceptions.correction: Track where the energy has gone rather than whether it has gone. Energy is conserved: what leaves the chemicals arrives in the surroundings and can be measured as a temperature rise.

misconceptions.question: An exothermic reaction transfers 200 kJ to the surroundings. How does the energy of the products compare with the reactants?
misconceptions.correct: The products have 200 kJ less energy than the reactants; the energy transferred out came from the chemicals.
misconceptions.misconception: The products have more energy than the reactants because the reaction released energy.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Released energy is read as gained energy, and exothermic reactions are associated with heat and flames, so students picture the products as the energy-rich end of the change.
misconceptions.correction: The energy given out has to come from somewhere, and it comes from the chemicals, so the products must sit lower in energy by exactly that amount.

misconceptions.question: Does conservation of energy mean the reactants and products have the same energy?
misconceptions.correct: No. Conservation applies to the universe as a whole; the products can be lower in energy provided the difference has gone to the surroundings.
misconceptions.misconception: Energy must balance on each side of the equation, so reactants and products have equal energy.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students transfer the rule they learned for conservation of mass, where both sides of a balanced equation carry the same atoms, onto energy without including the surroundings in the balance.
misconceptions.correction: Include the surroundings in the accounts. Chemicals plus surroundings is constant; chemicals alone are not.

misconceptions.question: A thermometer in a reaction mixture shows no change. Does that prove energy is conserved?
misconceptions.correct: Energy is always conserved. A steady temperature simply means little energy was transferred to or from the surroundings.
misconceptions.misconception: Conservation of energy means no energy is transferred during a reaction at all.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Conserved is heard as unchanged and then applied to each part separately, so students conclude that nothing can move between the chemicals and the surroundings.
misconceptions.correction: Conservation is about the total, not about each part. Energy moves freely between chemicals and surroundings while the total stays fixed.

misconceptions.question: A Bunsen flame is needed to light magnesium ribbon. Does that make the burning endothermic?
misconceptions.correct: No. Combustion is exothermic; the flame only supplies the energy needed to start the reaction.
misconceptions.misconception: Because energy has to be put in to start it, the reaction takes in energy overall and is endothermic.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students merge starting a reaction with the overall energy change, so any reaction that needs heating is filed as endothermic.
misconceptions.correction: Separate the start from the balance sheet. The energy needed to begin a reaction is the activation energy; the overall change is judged by whether the surroundings end up warmer or cooler.

misconceptions.question: What happens to the temperature when hydrochloric acid is neutralised by sodium hydroxide?
misconceptions.correct: It rises. Neutralisation is exothermic and transfers energy to the surroundings.
misconceptions.misconception: Neutralisation cancels the acid and the alkali out, so there is no energy change and no temperature change.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word neutral suggests nothing happening, and students picture the acid and alkali destroying each other rather than reacting to make a salt and water.
misconceptions.correction: Neutralisation is a chemical reaction that makes new substances, and it is one of the exothermic reactions named by the specification.

misconceptions.question: Iron powder rusting inside a hand warmer is a slow reaction. Does it still transfer energy?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. Oxidation of iron is exothermic, and the pack becomes noticeably warm.
misconceptions.misconception: Slow reactions with no flame transfer no energy to the surroundings.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Exothermic is associated with flames and explosions, so a quiet reaction with nothing to see is assumed to have no energy change.
misconceptions.correction: The specification lists many oxidation reactions as exothermic. Rate and energy change are separate: a slow reaction releases the same energy, just more gradually.

misconceptions.question: Which type of reaction is used in a self-heating can or a hand warmer?
misconceptions.correct: An exothermic reaction, which transfers energy to the drink or to the hands.
misconceptions.misconception: An endothermic reaction, because endothermic reactions release the heat they have stored.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Endo sounds like it should mean giving out, and students remember only that the device gets hot, not which way energy moves.
misconceptions.correction: Endothermic means energy is taken in from the surroundings, so the surroundings cool. Anything designed to warm something must use an exothermic reaction.

misconceptions.question: A hand warmer feels warm when you hold it. Where is the energy coming from?
misconceptions.correct: From the reaction inside the pack, which transfers energy to your hands.
misconceptions.misconception: The pack takes energy in from your hand and that is what makes it feel warm.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students know that heat flows between hand and object and pick the wrong direction, because taking in energy is loosely linked with anything to do with warmth.
misconceptions.correction: If energy flowed from your hand into the pack, your hand would feel colder. It feels warmer, so the pack is the source and the reaction is exothermic.

misconceptions.question: Where does the energy go in an exothermic reaction?
misconceptions.correct: Out of the chemicals into the surroundings, which is why the temperature of the surroundings increases.
misconceptions.misconception: It is stored inside the product molecules, which is why exothermic products are described as high in energy.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students meet stored chemical energy and place the energy in the products, missing that an exothermic reaction leaves the products lower in energy than the reactants.
misconceptions.correction: The energy transferred out is no longer in the chemicals. Exothermic products are lower in energy than the reactants, by the amount transferred out.

misconceptions.question: Copper carbonate must be heated strongly to decompose. Is the decomposition exothermic?
misconceptions.correct: No. Thermal decomposition is endothermic: energy is taken in from the surroundings for the compound to break down.
misconceptions.misconception: Because a hot flame is used, the reaction must be giving out energy and is exothermic.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The presence of heat is read as evidence of heat being produced, and the constant supply from the Bunsen makes it look as though the reaction is the source.
misconceptions.correction: Ask what happens if the flame is removed: the reaction stops, because it depends on energy being supplied. That is what endothermic means.

misconceptions.question: Citric acid reacts with sodium hydrogencarbonate and the mixture fizzes. What happens to the temperature?
misconceptions.correct: It falls. This reaction is endothermic and takes in energy from the surroundings.
misconceptions.misconception: The fizzing shows energy escaping, so the reaction must be exothermic.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Vigorous bubbling looks energetic, and students equate visible activity with energy being given out to the surroundings.
misconceptions.correction: Judge the direction from the thermometer, not from how lively the reaction looks. Here the reading falls, so energy has been taken in.

misconceptions.question: Why is an endothermic reaction chosen for a sports injury pack?
misconceptions.correct: Because it takes energy in from the surroundings, cooling the injured area and reducing swelling.
misconceptions.misconception: Sports packs warm the muscle, so the reaction inside them is exothermic.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Heat treatment for aching muscles is familiar, so students assume every sports pack is meant to warm rather than cool.
misconceptions.correction: The specification pairs injury packs with endothermic reactions. A fresh injury is cooled, and cooling means energy is taken from the surroundings.

misconceptions.question: The temperature of a reaction mixture rises. Have the chemicals gained energy?
misconceptions.correct: No. The chemicals have lost energy and the surroundings, which include the solution, have gained it.
misconceptions.misconception: A rising thermometer shows the chemicals taking energy in, so the reaction is endothermic.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students see the reading go up and attribute the gain to the reaction rather than to the surroundings that the thermometer is actually in.
misconceptions.correction: The thermometer reads the surroundings. Surroundings up means chemicals down, and the reaction is exothermic.

misconceptions.question: One reaction warms the surroundings by 2 °C and another by 20 °C. Which is exothermic?
misconceptions.correct: Both. Any rise in the temperature of the surroundings shows an exothermic reaction, whatever its size.
misconceptions.misconception: Only a large temperature change counts as exothermic; a small change means no real energy transfer.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students judge by how impressive the change looks rather than by its direction, so small rises are dismissed as experimental error.
misconceptions.correction: The direction of the change decides exothermic or endothermic; the size only tells you how much energy was transferred.

misconceptions.question: Why is a polystyrene cup with a lid used in Required practical 4?
misconceptions.correct: To reduce the energy transferred between the mixture and the surroundings, so the temperature change measured is closer to the true value.
misconceptions.misconception: The cup and lid make the reaction go faster so a temperature change can be seen.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Any piece of apparatus is assumed to be there to make the reaction work better, and insulation is not recognised as being about the accuracy of the measurement.
misconceptions.correction: The cup does not touch the chemistry; it insulates. Its job is to stop energy leaking to the bench and the air so the reading reflects the reaction.

misconceptions.question: In Required practical 4 a student adds different volumes of alkali to acid and records the temperature. Which is the independent variable?
misconceptions.correct: The volume of alkali added, because that is what the student deliberately changes.
misconceptions.misconception: The temperature is the independent variable because it is the important measurement.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students pick the variable they care about most, or the one written first in the results table, rather than the one they set themselves.
misconceptions.correction: The independent variable is the one you choose and change; the dependent variable is the one you measure as a result. Here you set the volume and read the temperature.

misconceptions.question: What does the activation energy of a reaction tell you?
misconceptions.correct: The minimum energy colliding particles must have for the reaction to occur.
misconceptions.misconception: It is the total energy given out by the reaction, the same as the overall energy change.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both quantities are marked on the same reaction profile, and students read whichever arrow they meet first without checking what it joins.
misconceptions.correction: The activation energy runs from the reactants up to the peak; the overall energy change runs from the reactants across to the products. Different arrows, different meanings.

misconceptions.question: Does an exothermic reaction have an activation energy?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. Every reaction has an activation energy, whether it gives out energy overall or takes it in.
misconceptions.misconception: Only endothermic reactions need an activation energy, since exothermic reactions give energy out.
misconceptions.whyItArises: If a reaction releases energy, students assume it cannot also require any, so they treat the activation energy as belonging to endothermic changes alone.
misconceptions.correction: Bonds in the reactants must be broken in every reaction, so every reaction needs a minimum energy to start. Petrol still needs a spark.

misconceptions.question: Two reactant particles collide. Does a reaction always follow?
misconceptions.correct: No. A reaction happens only if the particles collide with at least the activation energy.
misconceptions.misconception: Every collision between reactant particles produces a reaction.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Collision theory is remembered as particles must collide, and the second condition about sufficient energy is dropped.
misconceptions.correction: The specification requires both conditions: particles must collide with each other and with sufficient energy. A gentle collision simply bounces apart.

misconceptions.question: On a reaction profile for an exothermic reaction, where are the products drawn?
misconceptions.correct: Below the reactants, because the products are lower in energy by the amount transferred out.
misconceptions.misconception: Above the reactants, because an exothermic reaction gives out a lot of energy.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Higher on the diagram is read as more energy released, so students draw the bigger arrow upwards instead of tracking where the energy ends up.
misconceptions.correction: Height on the profile is the energy of the chemicals. Energy transferred out of the chemicals leaves the products lower down.

misconceptions.question: How is the activation energy shown on a reaction profile?
misconceptions.correct: As the rise from the reactants line up to the top of the curve.
misconceptions.misconception: It is the height of the peak measured from the bottom axis of the diagram.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students measure heights from the axis out of habit with graphs, rather than from the reactants line where the reaction starts.
misconceptions.correction: The activation energy is a difference, not a height above zero: measure from the reactants up to the peak.

misconceptions.question: What shape of line joins the reactants and products on a reaction profile?
misconceptions.correct: A curved line rising from the reactants over a peak and then falling to the products.
misconceptions.misconception: A straight sloping line drawn directly from the reactants to the products.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students think of the diagram as a graph of two energy levels and join them with a ruler, leaving out the activation energy barrier entirely.
misconceptions.correction: The specification asks for a curved line showing the energy as the reaction proceeds, which must pass over the activation energy peak.

misconceptions.question: What happens to the energy when a bond in a reactant molecule is broken?
misconceptions.correct: Energy must be supplied to break it, so bond breaking takes energy in.
misconceptions.misconception: Breaking a bond releases the energy that was stored in it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Everyday breaking is destructive and seems to let something out, and students imagine energy stored in the bond like a compressed spring.
misconceptions.correction: A bond is an attraction that must be pulled apart, and pulling anything apart against attraction costs energy. Breaking takes in, making gives out.

misconceptions.question: What happens to the energy when a bond in a product molecule is formed?
misconceptions.correct: Energy is released when bonds in the products are formed.
misconceptions.misconception: Energy has to be supplied to make new bonds, in the same way as for breaking them.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Making something sounds like work that must cost energy, so students apply the same sign to both processes and end up with no overall change.
misconceptions.correction: The two processes are opposite: breaking bonds takes energy in, forming bonds gives energy out. If both cost energy, no reaction could ever be exothermic.

misconceptions.question: How is the overall energy change worked out from bond energies?
misconceptions.correct: Energy needed to break bonds in the reactants minus energy released when bonds in the products form.
misconceptions.misconception: Bonds formed minus bonds broken, which reverses the sign of the answer.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The subtraction is remembered as products minus reactants from other calculations, so students take the sums in the wrong order.
misconceptions.correction: Work in the order the reaction happens: break first, make second. Break minus make gives a negative answer for an exothermic reaction.

misconceptions.question: In an exothermic reaction, which is greater: the energy needed to break bonds or the energy released forming them?
misconceptions.correct: The energy released from forming new bonds is greater than the energy needed to break existing bonds.
misconceptions.misconception: The energy needed to break bonds is greater, which is why energy is given out.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Exothermic is linked with lots of energy, and the breaking term is the one students meet first, so it is assumed to be the larger of the two.
misconceptions.correction: Whichever term is larger decides the direction. More energy out on making than in on breaking leaves a surplus that goes to the surroundings.

misconceptions.question: A reaction breaks four bonds and forms four bonds. Can it still be exothermic?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. What matters is the energy of the bonds, not how many are broken and formed.
misconceptions.misconception: The reaction must be neither exothermic nor endothermic, since the numbers of bonds match.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Counting bonds is easier than adding bond energies, so students balance the tally and assume the energies must balance too.
misconceptions.correction: Different bonds have different bond energies. Four strong bonds formed can release far more than four weak bonds needed to break.

misconceptions.question: A student adds every bond energy in the table together. What has gone wrong?
misconceptions.correct: Reactant bond energies and product bond energies must be summed separately and then subtracted.
misconceptions.misconception: All the bond energies are added to give one total energy for the reaction.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Addition feels safer than subtraction, and students lose track of which bonds belong to the reactants and which to the products.
misconceptions.correction: Make two sums: one for bonds broken and one for bonds formed. The overall energy change is the difference between them.

misconceptions.question: In H2 + Cl2 → 2HCl, how much energy is released as the H-Cl bonds form?
misconceptions.correct: Two moles of H-Cl are formed, so it is 2 x 431 = 862 kJ, not 431 kJ.
misconceptions.misconception: Each bond energy in the table is used once, whatever the balancing numbers in the equation say.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The table gives one value per type of bond, so students treat it as a list of quantities to use once each and never go back to the balanced equation to count how many of each bond there actually are.
misconceptions.correction: List the bonds in every molecule first, using the balancing numbers, then multiply each bond energy by the number of that bond present.

mcqs.stem: A reaction transfers energy to the surroundings. What must be true of the product molecules?

options.text: They have less energy than the reactants, by the amount transferred out.
options.rationale: This is the specification's own statement: the energy that reached the surroundings came from the chemicals, so the products sit lower by exactly that amount.

options.text: They have more energy than the reactants, by the amount given out.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who read released energy as gained energy and picture the products as the energy-rich end.

options.text: They have less energy, and the energy released no longer exists.
options.rationale: Half right about the products, but it treats the transferred energy as used up rather than moved to the surroundings.

options.text: They have exactly the same total energy as the reactants did.
options.rationale: Conservation of mass balances both sides of an equation, and the same bookkeeping is applied to energy, leaving the surroundings out.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about energy during a chemical reaction is correct?

options.text: No energy is transferred to or from the surroundings at all.
options.rationale: Wrong: thinking conservation means nothing moves, they deny any transfer to the surroundings.

options.text: The total energy in the universe is the same after the reaction as before.
options.rationale: Energy is conserved in chemical reactions; the reaction only moves energy between the chemicals and their surroundings.

options.text: Some of the energy is destroyed as the surroundings are being warmed.
options.rationale: Lost as heat is taken literally, so the energy leaves the accounts instead of appearing in the surroundings.

options.text: Reactants and products always contain exactly equal energy.
options.rationale: Wrong: a student believing reactants and products hold equal energy assumes their energies are identical.

mcqs.stem: Which statement describes an exothermic reaction?

options.text: It takes in energy from the surroundings, so their temperature rises.
options.rationale: Mixes the correct temperature change with the wrong direction of transfer, which is the commonest form of the exo/endo reversal.

options.text: It transfers energy out, so the temperature of the surroundings falls.
options.rationale: Right about the direction of transfer but reads the thermometer as belonging to the chemicals rather than the surroundings.

options.text: It transfers energy to the surroundings, so their temperature rises.
options.rationale: This is the specification definition: energy goes out to the surroundings and the temperature of the surroundings increases.

options.text: It stores the energy inside the products, so nothing warms up.
options.rationale: Comes from the idea of energy stored in chemicals, missing that exothermic products are lower in energy.

mcqs.stem: Which of these reactions is exothermic?

options.text: the thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate
options.rationale: Chosen by students who assume that a reaction carried out in a hot flame must be giving energy out.

options.text: the reaction inside a sports injury cold pack
options.rationale: Sports packs are associated with soothing heat, so the endothermic reaction inside them is misfiled as exothermic.

options.text: citric acid reacting with sodium hydrogencarbonate
options.rationale: The vigorous fizzing looks energetic, so students read visible activity as energy being given out.

options.text: the neutralisation of an acid by an alkali
options.rationale: Neutralisation is one of the three exothermic examples named by the specification, alongside combustion and many oxidation reactions.

mcqs.stem: Magnesium ribbon is lit with a Bunsen flame and burns brightly, warming the tripod above it. Why is this reaction described as exothermic?

options.text: Energy had to be supplied by the flame, so energy is taken in overall here.
options.rationale: Confuses the energy needed to start a reaction with the overall energy change of that reaction.

options.text: Combustion transfers energy to the surroundings, and that is why the tripod warms.
options.rationale: Combustion is exothermic; the flame only starts it, and the energy warming the tripod comes out of the chemicals.

options.text: The oxidation takes in energy from the surrounding air, making it glow.
options.rationale: Keeps the observation but reverses the transfer, treating the bright glow as energy arriving in the chemicals.

options.text: Burning stores the energy in the magnesium oxide that is produced.
options.rationale: Places the energy in the product, when an exothermic reaction leaves the product lower in energy.

mcqs.stem: A hand warmer contains iron powder that oxidises slowly once the pack is opened. Why does the pack become warm?

options.text: The pack takes energy in from your own hand, and this is what makes it warm.
options.rationale: Gets the direction of the transfer backwards; if this were true the hand would feel colder.

options.text: The reaction is endothermic, so it lets out the heat it had stored.
options.rationale: Uses the word endothermic while describing energy coming out, a sign the two terms have been swapped.

options.text: The oxidation is exothermic and transfers energy to your hands and the air.
options.rationale: Many oxidation reactions are exothermic, and the specification names hand warmers as an everyday use of one.

options.text: Slow reactions give out no energy; the padding keeps hands warm.
options.rationale: Assumes that a quiet reaction with no flame cannot transfer energy to the surroundings.

mcqs.stem: Which statement describes an endothermic reaction?

options.text: It takes in energy from the surroundings, so their temperature will rise.
options.rationale: Keeps the correct direction of transfer but attaches the wrong temperature change to it.

options.text: It gives out energy, and so the temperature of the surroundings falls.
options.rationale: Right about the falling thermometer but wrong about which way the energy moves.

options.text: It releases the energy that was stored inside the reactants.
options.rationale: Describes an exothermic change under the endothermic heading, a straight swap of the two terms.

options.text: It takes energy in from the surroundings, so their temperature falls.
options.rationale: This is the specification definition: energy is taken in from the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings decreases.

mcqs.stem: Copper carbonate is heated strongly and breaks down into copper oxide and carbon dioxide. Why is this reaction endothermic?

options.text: Energy is taken in to break the compound down.
options.rationale: Thermal decompositions are endothermic: energy has to be supplied continuously from the surroundings for the compound to break down.

options.text: Energy is given out because a hot flame is used here.
options.rationale: Reads the presence of heating as evidence that the reaction itself is producing heat.

options.text: Energy is stored, then released as the gas escapes.
options.rationale: Treats the carbon dioxide bubbling off as energy leaving, which is a visual rather than a thermal argument.

options.text: Energy is destroyed as the carbonate breaks apart.
options.rationale: Explains the missing energy by removing it from the universe instead of transferring it into the chemicals.

mcqs.stem: Citric acid solution is stirred with sodium hydrogencarbonate. The mixture fizzes and the thermometer falls from 21 °C to 15 °C. What does this show?

options.text: The reaction is exothermic, as the fizzing shows energy leaving.
options.rationale: Judges the direction from how lively the reaction looks rather than from the thermometer.

options.text: The reaction is exothermic, since the chemicals have lost energy.
options.rationale: Correctly notes a fall but assigns it to the chemicals, when the thermometer reads the surroundings.

options.text: The reaction is endothermic and takes energy in from the surroundings.
options.rationale: The temperature of the surroundings has decreased, which is the specification's test for an endothermic reaction; this pair is its named example.

options.text: No energy was transferred, as 6 °C is too small a change.
options.rationale: Dismisses a modest change as error; direction, not size, decides exothermic or endothermic.

mcqs.stem: A student measures the temperature of the surroundings before and after four reactions. Which result shows an endothermic reaction?

options.text: The temperature rose from 22.0 °C to 31.5 °C during this reaction.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who have the two terms the wrong way round and expect endothermic mixtures to warm.

options.text: The temperature rose from 16.5 °C to 22.0 °C as it went along.
options.rationale: The same reversal dressed up with a smaller rise; any rise shows an exothermic reaction.

options.text: The temperature stayed at 22.0 °C throughout the reaction.
options.rationale: Treats no measurable change as energy being taken in, when it shows very little transfer either way.

options.text: The temperature fell from 22.0 °C to 16.5 °C during the reaction.
options.rationale: A fall in the temperature of the surroundings is exactly how the specification says an endothermic reaction is recognised.

mcqs.stem: During a neutralisation the thermometer in the mixture rises by 8 °C. What has happened to the energy?

options.text: It has been transferred from the chemicals to the surroundings.
options.rationale: The solution is part of the surroundings, so a rise in its temperature shows energy leaving the chemicals: an exothermic reaction.

options.text: It has been transferred from the surroundings and into the chemicals.
options.rationale: The classic reversal: the rising reading is credited to the chemicals rather than to the surroundings being measured.

options.text: The chemicals still hold the very same energy they had before.
options.rationale: Wrong: believing reactant and product energies are equal, they deny any change despite the temperature rise.

options.text: It has been stored in the salt and the water that are made.
options.rationale: Places the energy in the products, when an exothermic reaction leaves them lower in energy.

mcqs.stem: A sports injury pack and a hand warmer each rely on a chemical reaction. Which comparison is correct?

options.text: The injury pack is exothermic; the hand warmer is endothermic.
options.rationale: Comes from assuming that all sports treatments are meant to warm the muscle.

options.text: The injury pack is endothermic and the warmer exothermic.
options.rationale: The pack must take energy in from the surroundings to cool a swelling, while the warmer must transfer energy out to the hands.

options.text: Both are exothermic, but the injury pack releases energy slowly.
options.rationale: Keeps the idea that the pack warms the skin and explains the cooling away as a slow release.

options.text: Both are endothermic, and each takes energy from the skin.
options.rationale: Treats warmth felt by the hand as energy flowing into the pack rather than out of it.

mcqs.stem: A self-heating can warms coffee using the reaction of calcium oxide with water. Which property makes this reaction suitable for that use?

options.text: It is endothermic, so it draws energy out of the air and into the drink.
options.rationale: Uses the wrong term while describing energy arriving in the drink, the usual sign of a swap.

options.text: It is exothermic, so the reacting chemicals themselves become hotter.
options.rationale: Right about the type of reaction but keeps the energy inside the chemicals instead of transferring it out.

options.text: It is exothermic, but only when the temperature change is large.
options.rationale: Makes the classification depend on the size of the change rather than its direction.

options.text: It is exothermic, so it transfers enough energy to warm the drink in the can.
options.rationale: An everyday use of an exothermic reaction: energy released by the reaction passes into the drink and raises its temperature.

mcqs.stem: In Required practical 4 a student adds different volumes of sodium hydroxide to 25 cm3 of acid and records the highest temperature reached. What is the independent variable?

options.text: the volume of sodium hydroxide added
options.rationale: It is the variable the student deliberately chooses and changes; the highest temperature is what is measured as a result.

options.text: the highest temperature that is reached
options.rationale: Picks the measurement the student cares about most, which is in fact the dependent variable.

options.text: the temperature of the acid before mixing
options.rationale: Wrong: fixating on temperature as the key measurement, they pick a temperature as independent.

options.text: the insulation of the plastic cup
options.rationale: Confuses a feature of the apparatus, kept constant to make the readings fair, with the variable being changed.

mcqs.stem: Why is the reacting mixture in Required practical 4 placed in a polystyrene cup with a lid?

options.text: to make the reaction happen faster inside the insulated cup
options.rationale: Wrong: believing the insulated cup speeds the reaction rather than reducing energy transfer.

options.text: to reduce the energy transferred to and from the surroundings
options.rationale: Polystyrene insulates and the lid limits evaporation, so more of the energy change shows up as a temperature change in the mixture.

options.text: to make the reaction go faster so that a change can be seen sooner
options.rationale: Assumes any apparatus must be there to help the reaction along rather than to protect the measurement.

options.text: to stop the temperature of the room from changing at all
options.rationale: Misplaces the surroundings outside the cup, when the mixture itself is what the thermometer measures.

mcqs.stem: Two reactant particles collide with each other but no reaction takes place. What is the reason?

options.text: Every collision must react, so this cannot happen.
options.rationale: Remembers collision theory as particles must collide and drops the condition about sufficient energy.

options.text: They collided with less than the energy given out here.
options.rationale: Substitutes the overall energy change for the activation energy; the two are different arrows on a profile.

options.text: They collided with too little energy to react.
options.rationale: Reactions occur only when particles collide with sufficient energy; a collision below the activation energy simply bounces apart.

options.text: The reaction is exothermic, so no energy is needed.
options.rationale: Assumes a reaction that gives energy out cannot also require energy to get started.

mcqs.stem: What is meant by the activation energy of a reaction?

options.text: the minimum amount of energy that particles must have in order to react
options.rationale: This is the specification's definition of the activation energy, word for word in substance.

options.text: the height of the peak measured from the bottom axis of the diagram
options.rationale: Reads a height on the profile as the activation energy instead of the rise from reactants to peak.

options.text: the total amount of energy the reaction gives out overall
options.rationale: Swaps the activation energy for the overall energy change, the other quantity marked on a profile.

options.text: the energy released whenever two reactant particles collide
options.rationale: Treats every collision as productive and as a source of energy rather than a requirement.

mcqs.stem: Which set of quantities can be shown on a reaction profile?

options.text: the temperature change, provided it is large enough to count as a real energy transfer
options.rationale: A reaction profile has no time axis; the horizontal direction shows the progress of the reaction.

options.text: the relative energies of the reactants and products, the activation energy and the overall energy change
options.rationale: These are precisely the three things the specification says a reaction profile can be used to show.

options.text: the activation energy on its own, because the products are not marked anywhere on the diagram
options.rationale: Remembers the peak but not that both energy levels are drawn, so the overall change is lost.

options.text: the rise in temperature, showing the energy that the chemicals have taken in
options.rationale: Wrong: reading a temperature rise as energy taken in, they expect it plotted on the profile.

mcqs.stem: A student draws a reaction profile for an endothermic reaction. Which description of the drawing is correct?

options.text: The products line lies below the reactants, joined by a curve with a peak.
options.rationale: Draws the exothermic shape, having read energy taken in as energy given out.

options.text: A straight sloping line runs from the reactants line up to the products.
options.rationale: Joins the two levels with a ruler and leaves out the activation energy barrier altogether.

options.text: The products line lies above the reactants, joined by a curved peak.
options.rationale: Endothermic products are higher in energy than the reactants, and the specification asks for a curved line passing over the activation energy peak.

options.text: The top of the curve is level with the products line on the right.
options.rationale: Merges the peak with the product energy, so the activation energy disappears from the diagram.

mcqs.stem: A reaction profile shows the products at a lower energy than the reactants. What does this tell you about the reaction?

options.text: It is endothermic and takes in energy overall.
options.rationale: Reads the drop from reactants to products as energy being absorbed by the chemicals.

options.text: It is exothermic only if the peak is low.
options.rationale: Makes the classification depend on the activation energy rather than on the two energy levels.

options.text: It cannot happen, as products must be higher.
options.rationale: Assumes every profile must rise, so a falling one is treated as a drawing error.

options.text: It is exothermic and gives out energy.
options.rationale: Products lower than reactants means the chemicals have lost energy, and that energy has gone to the surroundings.

mcqs.stem: Why must colliding particles have at least the activation energy?

options.text: because it is the energy the reaction gives to the surroundings
options.rationale: Describes the overall energy change, which is an output of the reaction rather than a requirement.

options.text: because it is the energy that is needed for the reaction to occur
options.rationale: The specification puts it in exactly these terms: the activation energy is the energy needed for a reaction to occur.

options.text: because it is only needed when a reaction is endothermic
options.rationale: Restricts the requirement to one type of reaction, when every reaction has an activation energy.

options.text: because it is the energy needed to make particles collide
options.rationale: Places the energy requirement on the collision itself rather than on the reaction that may follow.

mcqs.stem: During a chemical reaction, what happens to the bonds in the reactants?

options.text: Energy is released as each one of them breaks.
options.rationale: The most common bond-energy error: breaking is imagined to let out energy stored in the bond.

options.text: They break with no energy change at all.
options.rationale: Treats bond breaking as free, which would leave activation energy with nothing to do.

options.text: Energy must be supplied so that they break.
options.rationale: The specification states that energy must be supplied to break bonds in the reactants, so bond breaking takes energy in.

options.text: They break, and forming new bonds also takes energy.
options.rationale: Wrong: thinking forming bonds also needs energy in, like breaking them.

mcqs.stem: What happens to energy when the bonds in the products are formed?

options.text: Energy is released only if it is exothermic.
options.rationale: Makes bond forming conditional on the overall change, when forming always releases energy.

options.text: Energy must be supplied to make them form.
options.rationale: Applies the same sign to making bonds as to breaking them, which would rule out exothermic reactions.

options.text: Energy is stored and none gets out.
options.rationale: Locks the energy inside the product molecules instead of transferring it to the surroundings.

options.text: Energy is released as these bonds form.
options.rationale: The specification states that energy is released when bonds in the products are formed.

mcqs.stem: A student is given a table of bond energies for a reaction. What can these values be used to calculate?

options.text: the energy taken in breaking bonds and released forming them
options.rationale: Bond energies give both sums the specification names: the energy needed to break bonds and the energy released when bonds are formed.

options.text: the total energy of the reaction, by adding up every value in the table
options.rationale: Adds instead of grouping the values into a reactant sum and a product sum.

options.text: the number of bonds broken and the number of bonds formed in total
options.rationale: Counts bonds rather than energies, so strong and weak bonds are treated alike.

options.text: the temperature rise, showing the energy the chemicals take in
options.rationale: Wrong: treating a temperature rise as energy taken in, they think bond energies give it.

mcqs.stem: How is the overall energy change of a reaction found from bond energies?

options.text: the sum of the energy released forming bonds minus the sum needed to break
options.rationale: The subtraction the right way round in size but reversed in order, so the sign comes out wrong.

options.text: the sum of the energy needed to break bonds added to the sum released
options.rationale: Adds the two sums, giving a large positive number for every reaction.

options.text: the sum of the energy needed to break bonds minus the sum released forming bonds
options.rationale: This is the specification's definition of the overall energy change: the difference between the two sums, taken in that order.

options.text: the number of bonds broken subtracted from the number of bonds made
options.rationale: Counts bonds instead of adding bond energies, ignoring how strong each bond is.

mcqs.stem: H2 + Cl2 → 2HCl. Bond energies in kJ/mol: H–H 436, Cl–Cl 242, H–Cl 431. What is the overall energy change?

options.text: +1540 kJ/mol, adding all the values up
options.rationale: Adds 436 + 242 + 862 instead of subtracting the product sum from the reactant sum.

options.text: +184 kJ/mol, so it is endothermic
options.rationale: The right size from the right sums, but taken as forming minus breaking, which flips the sign.

options.text: +247 kJ/mol, using one H-Cl bond
options.rationale: Uses 678 - 431, forgetting that two moles of H-Cl bonds are formed.

options.text: -184 kJ/mol, so this is exothermic
options.rationale: Breaking: 436 + 242 = 678. Forming: 2 x 431 = 862. Overall energy change = 678 - 862 = -184 kJ/mol, so energy is given out.

mcqs.stem: In an exothermic reaction, how do the two bond energy sums compare?

options.text: Forming new bonds releases more than breaking bonds needs.
options.rationale: The specification states that in an exothermic reaction the energy released from forming new bonds is greater than the energy needed to break existing bonds.

options.text: Breaking existing bonds needs more than forming new bonds gives out.
options.rationale: The reversal that describes an endothermic reaction; the surplus would then have to be taken in.

options.text: More bonds are formed in the products than are broken overall.
options.rationale: Counts bonds rather than comparing energies, so bond strength is ignored.

options.text: The two sums are equal, so no energy is left over here.
options.rationale: Leaves no surplus at all, which would mean no energy could be transferred to the surroundings.

mcqs.stem: A reaction is endothermic. What does this tell you about the bond energy sums?

options.text: More bonds are broken than are formed in this reaction.
options.rationale: Compares numbers of bonds instead of the energies involved in each.

options.text: Breaking bonds needs more than forming lets out.
options.rationale: The specification states that in an endothermic reaction the energy needed to break existing bonds is greater than the energy released from forming new bonds.

options.text: Forming bonds gives out more than breaking needs.
options.rationale: Describes an exothermic reaction, the reversal of the two sums.

options.text: Forming new bonds takes in energy, making it endothermic.
options.rationale: Wrong: believing bond forming absorbs energy, they mislabel the cause of endothermicity.
